strengths: Proposes a biologically motivated graph contrastive learning method that directly leverages real gene knockdown perturbation data as supervision, addressing a meaningful mismatch between artificial augmentations and biological reality in GRN representation learning.

Provides a unified probabilistic formulation that incorporates supervised augmentation selection into KL-based contrastive learning and shows that standard node-level GCL can be recovered as a limiting case when the augmentation temperature goes to infinity.

Evaluates the method on real-world GRNs from three cancer types across both node-level (gene function and cancer relevance) and graph-level (hazard and subtype) downstream tasks, using public TCGA and LINCS datasets.
Includes substantial supplementary material on data preprocessing, GRN construction, hyperparameter tuning, and additional metrics, which supports transparency of the experimental pipeline.
Openly acknowledges a key limitation, namely that teacher GRNs were constructed from knockdown experiments of the same cancer type, and outlines future work toward broader generalization.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim of consistent superiority is not convincingly supported: performance gains are often small and within one standard deviation of baselines, and the paper reports no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals for the differences.

There is no ablation study isolating the contributions of the proposed components (e.g., Loss_Aug, supervised augmentation distribution, teacher embeddings). It is therefore unclear whether gains come from biological supervision or from extra regularization/training.

The theoretical derivation has notable gaps. The theorem assumes an unjustified independence structure p(i,j,a,b)=p(i,j)p(a,b), and the appendix KL decomposition appears to ignore or incorrectly handle marginal terms. Since both p_phi and q_phi are parameterized by the same GNN, the trivial-solution concern is not fully resolved theoretically.

The baselines are limited to self-supervised or reconstruction-based GCL methods. There is no supervised baseline that directly uses the knockdown data, no random-label control, and no alternative biological supervision, making it difficult to assess the unique value of the proposed supervision.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or trained model release is mentioned, GRN construction relies on specialized INGOR/SiGN-BN software and Fugaku-scale computation, and key implementation details such as data splits, random seeds, and the sampling-based estimators are not fully specified.

The paper has several presentation issues, including typos, inconsistent notation, and missing details in the main text (e.g., exact weighting of the two loss terms, alignment of teacher GRNs across datasets), which reduce clarity and make some claims hard to verify.

Generality is not demonstrated beyond same-cancer-type teacher GRNs. Cross-cancer or cross-cell-line transfer is not tested, so the practical reach of the method for broader GRN representation learning remains unclear.

Downstream evaluation concerns remain: gene-level labels are highly imbalanced, cancer-related classification relies on undersampling that may not reflect realistic deployment, and there is no external validation cohort to test robustness.

strengths: Novel and biologically motivated idea: using real gene knockdown perturbation (teacher GRNs from LINCS) as supervision for augmentation-level contrastive learning on GRNs is a fresh, underexplored direction compared to artificial augmentations, and it is well situated within the graph representation learning for biology literature.

Principled framing: building the method on the I-Con (KL-divergence) contrastive framework yields a clean two-term objective (node-level loss under a supervised augmentation distribution + augmentation-level distribution matching), and the decomposition in Theorem 1 is at least correctly derived under the stated independence assumption.

Breadth of empirical setup: 3 cancer types (breast/lung/colorectal), 13 node- and graph-level tasks (BP/CC/cancer-relevance, hazard/subtype), with real TCGA and LINCS data and a substantial appendix documenting data acquisition, GO/OncoKB labeling, GRN estimation, and hyperparameters.

Qualitative analyses add value: the t-SNE/PCA latent-space diagnostics (including the PCA evidence of GraphCL dimensional collapse at 98.3% PC1 variance) and the embedding-dimension sweep are informative and go beyond simple leaderboard reporting.

The limitations section honestly acknowledges that teacher GRNs were only available within the same cancer type, and the paper is transparent that gains are not statistically significant on every task.
weaknesses: Central claim is not supported by the evidence: nearly all reported improvements lie within one standard deviation of the baselines (e.g., BP Breast 0.243±0.052 vs w/o-pretrain 0.232±0.031; Lung BP 0.282 vs 0.259; Rel. Breast 0.600 vs 0.580), many tasks are effectively ties, and some baselines regress to w/o-pretrain or below. No significance tests or multiple-comparison correction are reported, yet the abstract/intro/contribution list claim SupGCL 'consistently outperformed' and 'in all experiments SupGCL achieves better performance than state-of-the-art baselines'.

Unfair comparison: SupGCL consumes additional supervised information (gene-knockdown teacher GRNs) that none of the self-supervised baselines (GAE, GraphCL, GRACE, SGRL) have access to. There is no supervised baseline (e.g., direct use of knock-down labels), and no ablation isolating whether gains stem from the extra supervision or from the proposed biological augmentation modeling. Without this, the headline 'outperforms SOTA' claim is confounded.

Theoretical contribution is overstated and under-developed. Theorem 1 is a routine application of the KL chain rule under an assumed factorization p(i,j,a,b)=p(i,j)p(a,b), and Corollary 1 is a trivial limit showing uniform sampling is recovered as τ_a→∞. The statement that 'existing GCL methods are special cases' is therefore only a limiting-sampling observation, not a demonstration that GRACE/GraphCL/SGRL are recovered. Critically, both p_φ and q_φ are parameterized by the same GNN f_φ, so the 'reference' distribution is not fixed; the paper admits collapse is possible but only argues heuristically that the combined loss avoids it, with no proof or analysis of degenerate minima.

No ablation of the mechanism: the augmentation-level loss term, τ_a, and the specific augmentation design (zeroing node a's feature and its incident edges) are never isolated, so the claim that biological grounding of augmentations drives improvement is not empirically tested. It is also unclear how the text-specified augmentation relates to the 'teacher' GRN embedding beyond distribution matching.

Reproducibility and cost concerns: GRN structure estimation requires INGOR on the Fugaku supercomputer (up to 21 h on 528 nodes), plus ~9–21 h of pretraining per cancer type. Furthermore, the network structure is estimated once per cancer type and shared across patients (only features vary), which contradicts the paper's 'patient-specific/individualized GRN' framing and introduces large unaccounted shared variance that could dominate results.

Baseline tuning and presentation quality raise fairness/readability doubts: GraphCL collapsing to subset accuracy 0.115 suggests the baselines were not tuned to a comparable standard, and reported per-method hyperparameters (all temperatures fixed at 0.25) hint at limited search that may favor the proposed method. The manuscript also contains numerous presentation defects: equation-rendering errors (sin_F vs sim_F in Eq. 6), reference mismatches (GraphCL attributed to [13] 'Graph contrastive learning automated' while [9] is the actual GraphCL), inconsistent notation/Loss naming across body and appendix, and figure/caption confusion.

strengths: Novel and biologically motivated use of real gene knockdown perturbations from LINCS as supervision for graph contrastive learning on gene regulatory networks, addressing the mismatch between artificial augmentations and biological reality.

Provides a principled probabilistic formulation in which conventional node-level GCL is a special case when the augmentation temperature tau_a goes to infinity (Corollary 1), giving a unified view of supervised augmentation selection and GCL.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three cancer types (breast, lung, colorectal) and 13 downstream tasks at both node and graph levels, with comparisons to five baselines; SupGCL achieves the best main-table results across all reported tasks and datasets.

Includes useful additional analyses: t-SNE and PCA visualizations of latent spaces, additional metrics (Macro F1, Jaccard), embedding-dimension studies, and a detailed appendix covering datasets, network estimation, hyperparameters, and compute environment.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported by public datasets (TCGA, LINCS), detailed preprocessing and network-estimation procedures, hyperparameter tables, and an explicit training algorithm.
weaknesses: The 'supervised' framing is somewhat overstated: the reference distribution p_phi(b|a) is parameterized by the same GNN as q_phi, so both the teacher and target distributions are learned jointly; the method is closer to a learned multi-view regularizer than to standard supervised learning with fixed labels.

The augmentation-level distributions use an unnormalized Frobenius inner product in the softmax (Eq. 6), which can be dominated by embedding norms and may lead to degenerate or trivial similarity distributions; standard contrastive learning typically uses cosine similarity.

Experimental gains are often modest and lack statistical significance tests, e.g., BP Breast subset accuracy 0.243±0.052 vs. 0.232±0.031 without pretraining; additional metrics show SupGCL sometimes underperforming baselines (e.g., BP Lung Macro F1 0.546 vs. GraphCL 0.584; BP Colorectal Jaccard 0.502 vs. 0.537 w/o pretrain), contradicting the abstract's claim that SupGCL achieves better performance in all experiments.

Scope is limited: only 975 landmark genes, three cancer types, and teacher GRNs constructed from the same cancer type; the paper does not demonstrate cross-cancer or external validation, and the resource-heavy INGOR/Fugaku network estimation may hinder reproducibility.

Presentation and notation have inconsistencies, including 'sin_F' vs. 'sim_F', unclear definition of p_phi(j,b|i,a), a terse proof in Appendix A, and potential typos in Algorithm 1 (e.g., line 10's z_i^* notation). There is also no discussion of broader societal or clinical-deployment risks beyond a single limitation statement.

strengths: Novel and biologically motivated idea: instead of avoiding graph augmentations, SupGCL treats real gene knockdown perturbations as supervision, turning structural changes into useful learning signals for GRNs.

Provides a probabilistic formulation that unifies node-level contrastive learning and augmentation-level supervision, with Theorem 1 decomposing the proposed loss into node-level GCL and augmentation-alignment terms.
Broad empirical evaluation across 13 downstream tasks, three cancer types, and both node-level and graph-level tasks; includes multiple baselines, latent-space visualization, and enrichment analysis.
Reports consistent improvements over several baselines and shows that SupGCL can learn representations that better separate breast cancer subtypes in t-SNE and clustering metrics.
Uses public datasets (TCGA, LINCS) and provides substantial implementation details, including hyperparameter search spaces and downstream fine-tuning protocols.

Includes an honest limitations discussion, especially the failure of cross-cancer fine-tuning, and provides robustness analyses over patient sample size, supervision sample size, and GRN filtering thresholds.
The biological enrichment analysis suggests that SupGCL embeddings can recover interpretable functional modules, which is a useful additional validation signal.
weaknesses: The central claim of consistently outperforming state-of-the-art methods is not statistically supported: most gains over the strongest baseline (GRACE) are within standard deviation, and significance testing only reports improvements over GraphCL and SGRL on a few node-level tasks, not over GRACE or all tasks.

The paper omits comparison with the most directly related GRN-specific GCL baseline, MuSe-GNN, which uses multimodal biological views as natural augmentations; this weakens the claimed state-of-the-art comparison.

The theoretical extension is largely a standard KL-divergence chain-rule decomposition. Corollary 1 does not rigorously show that conventional GCL is a special case because the augmentation set remains knockdown-based, not the arbitrary artificial augmentations used in conventional GCL.

The optimization setup is potentially unstable: p_phi is parameterized by the same GNN as q_phi, so the reference distribution is not fixed. The trivial-solution concern is acknowledged but not resolved with a stop-gradient, fixed teacher, or theoretical guarantee against collapse.

Reproducibility is limited by the GRN estimation pipeline: it relies on specialized INGOR/SiGN-BN Bayesian network estimation run on the Fugaku supercomputer, and no code release is mentioned. Re-running the full pipeline would be impractical for most groups.

The knockdown simulation is a crude approximation: setting node and edge features to zero does not model the graded, downstream, and context-dependent effects of real gene knockdown, which may limit biological faithfulness.

Teacher GRNs are derived from cell line knockdown experiments, while target graphs are patient-specific TCGA GRNs; the domain mismatch is apparent in the cross-domain fine-tuning failures and is not fully addressed by the model.
The method is evaluated only on 975 landmark genes, which restricts its scope and may not generalize to genome-scale GRNs.

The manuscript contains presentation and notation issues: e.g., X_{i,j}^V has conflicting indices, 'sin_F' is used for cosine similarity, 'contractive' is used for contrastive, and the algorithm pseudocode has apparent indexing errors in the softmax similarity terms.

Computational cost is substantial: SupGCL pre-training takes roughly 9--21 hours per cancer type on an H100, far more than most baselines, but scalability and cost trade-offs are not critically discussed.

strengths: The paper proposes a novel and biologically motivated idea: instead of treating augmentation-induced graph changes as a nuisance, it uses real gene knockdown perturbation data as supervision for graph contrastive learning on gene regulatory networks.

It offers a probabilistic formulation that links artificial augmentations with biological knockdown graphs, and Theorem 1/Corollary 1 provide a conceptual connection showing conventional node-level GCL as a limiting case when the augmentation-level temperature grows.

The empirical study is broad: 13 downstream tasks across three cancer types, node-level and graph-level evaluations, multiple baselines, and additional robustness, cross-domain, and biological enrichment analyses in the appendix.
The authors report additional metrics beyond accuracy (F1, Jaccard, NMI, ARI) and honestly discuss the failure of cross-cancer fine-tuning, which is a useful limitation disclosure.
weaknesses: The central claim that SupGCL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines is not supported by the evidence. Many improvements are within one standard deviation (e.g., breast hazard 0.650±0.059 vs GRACE 0.642±0.064; subtype 0.847±0.036 vs GRACE 0.841±0.026; BP lung 0.282±0.037 vs w/o-pretrain 0.259±0.056). Appendix F.4 reports only four significant differences, all against GraphCL or SGRL, and none against GAE, GRACE, or w/o-pretrain. In Appendix F.1 SupGCL is not best on several metrics (e.g., BP lung macro F1 0.546 vs GraphCL 0.584; CC lung macro F1 0.387 vs GAE 0.395; CC colorectal macro F1 0.397 vs GAE 0.403), contradicting the 'consistently outperforms' claim.

The theoretical formulation has important soundness issues. The reference distribution p_phi(b|a) is parameterized by the same trainable GNN f_phi as q_phi(b|a), so Loss_Aug minimizes a KL divergence between two trainable distributions. This can trivially collapse, as the authors acknowledge, and the added node-level loss does not theoretically prevent collapse at the augmentation level. Theorem 1 also relies on an averaging/joint-KL equivalence and independence/factorization assumptions that are only sketched and not rigorously justified.

The algorithm pseudocode contains errors that undermine reproducibility (e.g., q_phi(b|a) is computed from <Z^a,Z^a> and p_phi(b|a) from <Y^a,Y^a> instead of comparing against Z^c/Y^c; the node-level softmax appears to use <z^j,z^j>). These are not cosmetic and raise doubts about whether the implementation matches the formal objective.

Teacher GRN construction is critically underspecified. The method requires a separate teacher GRN H_a for each knockdown gene a, but Appendix D and Tables 7-8 report only one LINCS network per cancer type (e.g., breast LINCS: 975 nodes, 10,498 edges), not per knockdown target. It is unclear how thousands of knockdown experiments are aggregated into H_a, how node and edge features for H_a are defined, how genes without available knockdown data are handled, and what the effective set K is. This is central to the method and makes independent reproduction difficult.

The baselines are generic graph representation methods (GAE, GraphCL, GRACE, SGRL, w/o-pretrain) and omit domain-specific GRN representation methods (MuSe-GNN, GCLink, CancerGATE) from the main downstream comparisons, despite discussing them as directly relevant. GCLink is only compared in an appendix link-prediction experiment, so the claim of state-of-the-art GRN representation learning is not adequately supported.

There is a domain mismatch between supervision and evaluation: supervision comes from cancer cell line knockdown experiments (LINCS), while downstream tasks are on patient tumor GRNs (TCGA). The paper does not validate that the learned augmentation-level distribution captures patient-relevant biology, and Appendix G concedes that fine-tuning across cancer types is not robust, which limits practical significance.

The reported effect sizes are generally small, and the latent-space analysis shows only marginal improvements (e.g., NMI 0.117 for SupGCL vs 0.110 for GRACE; ARI 0.150 vs 0.134). This does not convincingly demonstrate a decisive advantage over strong baselines.

The 'supervised' aspect is weaker than claimed: supervision is applied only to the whole-graph augmentation-similarity distribution, not to node/gene-level perturbation effects. The rich knockdown data—which genes change expression after knockdown—is not directly used to align node embeddings, so the method may not exploit the biological supervision as effectively as the motivation suggests.

Reproducibility is limited beyond the pseudocode issues: no code or trained models are provided, several hyperparameter and preprocessing choices are unclear, and the GRN estimation relies on large-scale Fugaku computations without releasing the estimated intermediate networks. The paper also has presentation problems, including inconsistent notation (e.g., X_{i,j}^V for i-th gene, X_{i,j}^E for i-th edge) and 'sin_F' used for cosine similarity.

strengths: The paper proposes a novel and biologically motivated idea: using real gene knockdown perturbation data as supervision for graph contrastive learning on gene regulatory networks, directly challenging the augmentation-free trend that treats structural perturbations as noise to be avoided.

It provides a probabilistic formulation that unifies node-level GCL and augmentation-level supervision, with Theorem 1 decomposing the proposed loss into a supervised node-level contrastive term and an augmentation-level distribution-matching term, and Corollary 1 linking the method to conventional GCL in a limiting case.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: 13 downstream tasks across three cancer types, covering node-level gene function and cancer-related classification and graph-level hazard and subtype prediction, plus ablations on temperature, embedding dimension, robustness, cross-domain transfer, link prediction, and biological enrichment.

SupGCL achieves the best mean performance across all 13 reported tasks against strong baselines including GAE, GraphCL, GRACE, and the recent augmentation-free SGRL, with particularly clear gains on graph-level hazard prediction and breast-cancer subtype classification.

The paper includes useful reproducibility details: public TCGA and LINCS datasets, preprocessing steps, hyperparameter search spaces, model architecture, and computational environment, and it honestly discusses the failure to generalize across cancer types during fine-tuning.
The latent-space and GO/KEGG enrichment analyses provide biological interpretability evidence, suggesting that SupGCL embeddings capture meaningful functional modules and cancer-relevant pathways.
weaknesses: The central claim of consistent superiority over state-of-the-art baselines is overstated given the evidence: many improvements are small and within one standard deviation, and the reported Bonferroni-corrected significance tests show significant gains only over GraphCL and SGRL on a few node-level tasks, with no significant differences reported against GRACE, GAE, or the no-pretraining baseline.

The construction of the teacher GRNs is insufficiently described. The appendix appears to estimate one LINCS network per cancer type, but the method defines a separate teacher GRN H_a for each knockdown gene a; it is unclear how multiple knockdown experiments targeting the same gene are aggregated into H_a and how real perturbation graphs are represented. This harms reproducibility and interpretation.

There is a potential mismatch between artificial augmentations, which zero a gene's features and incident edges, and real knockdown experiments, which alter expression and downstream regulation without literally zeroing the gene. The method does not directly align artificial augmented embeddings Z^a with teacher embeddings Y^a; supervision enters only through a trainable reference distribution p_phi(b|a), which is parameterized by the same GNN as q_phi, deviating from standard contrastive learning where the reference is fixed.

Missing ablations weaken the empirical justification for the proposed contrastive machinery. There is no comparison to simpler supervised baselines such as direct MSE alignment between Z^a and Y^a, predicting the knockdown target, or other ways of using the same teacher graphs. It is therefore unclear whether the specific augmentation-level contrastive loss is necessary.

The theoretical novelty is modest: Theorem 1 is a standard KL decomposition under a strong independence assumption p(i,j,a,b)=p(i,j)p(a,b), and Corollary 1 is a limiting case that recovers node-level GCL only over the set K of knockdown operations, not necessarily conventional GCL over arbitrary augmentations.

The temperature ablation is noisy and does not show a clear monotonic trend toward GRACE as tau_a increases, so the empirical support for Corollary 1 is weak. In particular, hazard performance is best at tau_a=0.1 rather than at the default 0.25, and several metrics fluctuate non-monotonically.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: no code release is mentioned, and the GRN estimation relies on INGOR/SiGN-BN on the Fugaku supercomputer with long runtimes. The pseudocode in Appendix B is garbled and contains indexing/notation errors, making exact reimplementation difficult.

The evaluation is transductive: pre-training uses all patient graphs before downstream cross-validation, and this setting is not discussed. While common in graph SSL, it limits claims about inductive generalization to unseen patients or networks.

The biological enrichment analysis is qualitative and lacks statistical comparison across methods; conclusions such as SupGCL separating autophagy regulation versus execution could be sensitive to clustering choices and should be interpreted cautiously.

The presentation has several notation and typographical issues, e.g., X_{i,j}^V for a node feature, 'contractive' instead of 'contrastive', 'sin_F' instead of 'sim_F', and some reference-year mismatches, which reduce clarity.
